messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Violence: Violence, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sione is a 74-year-old editor who has spent the last four decades of his career in a small publishing house, proofreading manuscripts and fact-checking articles. He is a large man, broad-shouldered and soft-spoken, the kind of person colleagues describe as “gentle.” But they also find him distant. He rarely joins office lunches, never argues about editorial decisions, and if someone suggests a change to his work, he becomes very still and says nothing for a long moment before quietly agreeing. What his colleagues do not know is that the moment someone corrects him, the world splits into slides—a tight close-up of a woman’s hand, then a flash of light over the kitchen floor, then a sound he cannot name. He sees these pictures, but they do not feel like his own memory. They feel as though they belong to a different man, a man who was weak enough to let that happen.

The event that seeded this came thirty-five years ago, in the house he shared with his wife, a gifted violinist named Leilani. Their marriage had been passionate and volatile, and Sione had long believed that his own temperament—too placid, too accommodating—was what kept provoking her. When she struck him, he told himself it was his fault for being the sort of person who made her that angry. He told himself he must have deserved it. He became an object in those moments, something to be acted upon, and after she left—she left him, finally, for a cellist who matched her fire—he carried that objecthood inside him. He could not feel anything properly after that. Joy felt like a photograph someone else had taken. Grief was a distant hum. Rage, though, was real. When he remembered her hand, or the sound of a door slamming, a hot wave of fury would arrive unbidden. But even that rage felt foreign, as though it belonged to the other man, the one who should have defended himself and never did.

For years Sione managed by staying busy. Editing was perfect for this: every sentence needed his attention, every comma a small decision. He could lose himself in someone else’s story. He learned to stop reading the sections of manuscripts that described physical conflict—he would hand those pages to a junior editor without explanation. He stopped watching films with violent scenes. He stopped going to concerts, because the sight of a violinist on stage would tighten his throat. And most of all, he stopped letting himself feel anything strong. When a colleague praised his work, he nodded and changed the subject. When he felt loneliness at night, he turned on the television and watched cooking shows until his eyes blurred. Strong emotions were doorways to the snapshots, and he refused to walk through them.

The price of this was a slow erosion of his life outside work. His divorce had been inevitable—Leilani had left years before, but Sione had never pursued another relationship. He told himself he did not have the emotional capacity for it. His friendships became arrangements of shared activities: a weekly chess game with an old neighbor, but no talk of the past. By the time he was seventy, his social world had shrunk to his desk and the quiet evenings in his apartment. He was not unhappy, exactly. He was empty, and emptiness had become comfortable.

What finally brought him to a clinic was a single sentence from a new colleague, a young woman who handed back his edit of her article and said, “This whole paragraph is a mess—what were you thinking?” The words hit him like a slap. He saw the snapshots: a kitchen floor, a shattered cup, Leilani’s face above him. He felt the rage, hot and impossible, and then he felt his hand gripping the edge of the desk so hard his knuckles went white. He did not say a word. But that night, alone in his apartment, he admitted to himself that he had been holding his breath for thirty-five years. He wanted to know if he could breathe again, if he could feel normal emotions without being swamped by pictures that did not even feel like his own. He came to therapy because he was afraid that the alternative—continuing to live as an object, a body that edited manuscripts and avoided feelings—would leave him emptier still.
